generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, active revision matters because the discipline rewards knowledge you can use, not just recognise. Rereading a chapter on, say, memory models leaves the ideas feeling familiar, yet an exam asks you to reproduce a model, compare studies and apply findings. Rebuilding a theory from memory, sketching a study's design, and testing yourself on competing explanations force the deeper processing that recognition never reaches.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students set aside the same hours to revise the same topic: theories of attachment.

Tom spends the time reading. He reads the textbook chapter twice and highlights the key studies, from Bowlby to Ainsworth. It feels like steady progress, and he covers every page. But he produces nothing: no diagram of the theories, no self-test, no explanation in his own words. When a past question asks him to evaluate attachment theory, the material feels familiar yet strangely hard to reproduce. This is passive revision.

Amara reads the same chapter once, then closes it. She rebuilds the theories from memory as a comparison table, turns each gap into a test question, and explains the Strange Situation aloud into a recording. Each gap that surfaces sends her back to the chapter with a purpose. By the end she can reproduce and compare the theories, not just recognise them. This is active revision.

Both spent the same hours. Only Amara turned those hours into knowledge that would survive the exam, by producing and testing rather than only reading.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision in psychology is a different kind of work with your material, not just more time on it. You can now contrast active and passive revision and explain why producing and testing a theory deepens it, and you can judge whether an approach is truly active. The next lesson turns this into the specific techniques you can choose from.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's revision active rather than passive?

items.text: She rebuilt the theories from memory and tested herself, returning to the chapter only to fix gaps.
She spent more hours revising than Tom.
She read the chapter more carefully than Tom.
She highlighted the key studies in the textbook.

feedback.correct: That's right. Producing and testing the theories, then targeting the chapter, is what made it active.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID with the material, beyond reading it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara rebuilt the theories from memory and tested herself, returning to the chapter only to fix gaps. Extra hours, careful reading and highlighting are all still passive.
